newsitem.title: USA: Chicago's futures exchanges face challenges - study.
newsitem.headline: Chicago's futures exchanges face challenges - study.

text.p: Chicago's futures and options exchanges, which lost nearly half their global market share between 1987 and 1995, face numerous challenges that could continue to eat into their business.

"We are on the precipice of being hurt, and I think that's why we are stepping up to the plate and putting everyone on notice," Jack Sandner, chairman of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, said at a news conference.

A 400-page, six-part study sponsored by the Risk Management Center of Chicago said U.S. regulations, coupled with growth in over-the-counter markets and foreign markets, threatened Chicago's leadership role in risk management.

Volume at the Chicago exchanges grew to 574 million contracts in 1995, up 45 percent from the 396 million contracts traded in 1987, but their global market share fell to 31 percent from 60 percent in the same period, the study said.

Worldwide volume for exchange-traded products grew to 1.8 billion contracts in 1995 from 664 million in 1987, as the number of foreign futures and options exchanges increased dramatically, the study said.
The study also noted that over-the-counter markets have expanded sharply in the last 10 years, with the OTC derivatives markets rising to $17.7 trillion in 1995 from $500 billion in 1986.
However, at Monday's news conference held at Chicago's City Hall, exchange leaders and industry officials pointed to U.S. regulations as the number one threat to their business.
"No matter how much we strive for excellence, and no matter how fine a job that we do, it can be impacted by a non-nurturing regulatory environment," Sandner said.
The report cited a 1995 report from the London Business School that found the cost of U.S. regulation is 57 percent higher than in Britain.
"Regulations are needed, but they cannot be overburdensome and at an unnecessary cost," Chicago Mayor Richard Daley said at the press conference.
The Risk Management Center was established from a recommendation by the Chicago Civic Committee's 1987 report on the financial services industry.

The 1996 study recommended that Chicago exchanges cooperate even more to level the regulatory playing field with U.S. OTC markets and foreign futures markets. The study suggested cost-benefit analysis for tax and regulatory proposals.

A spokesman for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates exchange-traded futures and options products, said the CFTC had no comment on the study. ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters.com))
